nameStory: The oblong running spider gets its name from its distinctly elongated, stretched-out body shape that looks like someone gently pulled a typical spider from both ends. Unlike many spiders that sit and wait, this one actively runs and hunts its prey, giving it the 'running' part of its common name. It's also called the slender crab spider because it can move sideways like a crab and has that characteristic thin, oblong appearance.
description: The oblong running spider is a small, slender hunter that looks quite different from the round, plump spiders many people picture. Its body is notably elongated and narrow, almost stick-like, which helps it blend in perfectly among grass stems and plant stalks. This active predator doesn't build webs but instead roams through grassy areas hunting small insects. It's part of the running crab spider family, meaning it can scuttle sideways and backwards as easily as it moves forward.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly oblong and narrow body that feels surprisingly firm when gently touched, like a small twig - much more elongated than typical round spiders

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Actively runs and hunts rather than sitting in a web, often seen moving quickly through grass with a distinctive crab-like sideways scuttle

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web at all - this is a free-roaming hunter that relies on speed and stealth rather than silk traps

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to easily blend among grass blades, with the body length noticeably longer than it is wide

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Coloration tends to be muted browns and tans that match dried grass stems, often with subtle striping along the elongated abdomen

habitat: Look for oblong running spiders in grassy meadows, fields, and the edges of lawns throughout New England. They prefer areas with tall grasses and herbaceous plants where their slender bodies can easily hide among the vertical stems. You'll often find them in unmowed areas, prairie-like spaces, and weedy field margins where small insects are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning their hunting season in tall spring grasses and emerging wildflower areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily spotted actively hunting during daylight hours in meadows and grasslands.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to prepare for winter, often found lower in the grass structure as they seek protected overwintering spots.
seasonality.winter: Hidden in protected spots like grass tufts or under debris, essentially dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This spider's elongated body isn't just for show - it's perfectly evolved to mimic a grass stem or twig, and it will actually align its body with plant stalks and freeze motionless when threatened, becoming nearly invisible even when you're looking right at it!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with thin twigs or grass stems rather than other spiders! When it freezes in its camouflage position, even experienced naturalists can walk right past it. The key is watching for movement - real twigs don't suddenly scuttle sideways.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'crab spider,' the oblong running spider is actually in a different family (Philodromidae) than the true crab spiders (Thomisidae). Both groups earned the 'crab spider' name because they can move sideways, but running crab spiders are generally more active hunters while true crab spiders are more sit-and-wait ambush predators.
compareHints: The oblong running spider can be distinguished from its relative, the maritime running crab spider, primarily by habitat preference - the oblong prefers inland grassy areas while the maritime species is found in coastal environments. Both share the characteristic elongated body shape, but the maritime species is typically found near salt marshes and coastal vegetation rather than the meadows and grasslands where the oblong running spider thrives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Maritime Running Crab Spider is extremely similar to its close relative, the Oblong Running Spider, but habitat is the key difference - Maritime is found only in coastal salt-influenced areas while Oblong lives inland.
